cold-reader-runB.title: session_id vs workspace_id vs "collaboration" relationship never stated, and no session lifecycle
cold-reader-runB.quote:
| `session_id` | UUIDv7 for one collaboration |
| `workspace_id` | Random UUID for the logical workspace |
cold-reader-runB.problem: "Collaboration" appears at lines 46, 77, and 153 and is never defined; line 153 defines `session_id` in terms of it. The cardinality between `session_id` and `workspace_id` is never stated. Evidence pulls both ways: line 167-168 has one genesis record binding both, implying 1:1 forever; but then two IDs are redundant. Line 564 "matching `workspace_id`: resume" implies a workspace outlives something. Line 59 "session-lifetime coordination history with export before compaction" implies sessions *end* — but I grepped `end session|session end|archive|teardown|leave|retire`: there is no session-termination flow anywhere. §9's CLI (638-651) has `host` and `join` but no `leave`, `end`, or `archive`. Compounding this, "session" is also used for three other things in the same doc: `agent_session_id` (156), TLS/control "sessions" that revocation closes (253, 548), and "Syncthing sidecar per session" (533).
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: An implementer must decide whether a device can be in two sessions over one workspace, whether re-hosting the same directory next week is the same `session_id` (affecting the entire Raft log, credential history, and `.codecomm/state.db` reuse), and what "session-lifetime" history retention actually bounds. Guessing wrong means either a DB that grows forever with no defined truncation point, or a resume path that silently discards committed history. §13 phase 6 lists "backup/export/compaction" as deliverable work with no spec to build against.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: In §4.1 after line 160 add three sentences: the exact cardinality ("one workspace has exactly one live session; a workspace_id MAY be reused by a later session, a session_id never is" — or whatever is intended), a one-line definition of "collaboration", and a pointer to a new short subsection describing how a session ends (owner-initiated? last-member-departs?), what happens to `.codecomm/state.db`, and what "export before compaction" produces. Also pick one word: reserve "session" for the collaboration and rename the TLS/sidecar uses to "connection"/"per-collaboration sidecar".

cold-reader-runB.title: Worktree "publish" — the default isolation mode's only integration path — is one sentence
cold-reader-runB.quote:
- **Isolated worktree (default):** create a Git worktree outside Syncthing per
  launched agent. Publish a reviewed proposal containing base commit, paths,
  digests, and patch/commit metadata into the canonical synchronized tree.
cold-reader-runB.problem: Line 28 makes isolated worktrees the default, so this is the primary path by which agent work becomes shared work, and it gets three lines. I grepped `patch|base commit|canonical synchronized tree|publish`: lines 508-510 and the CLI verb at 639 are the whole treatment. "Canonical synchronized tree" is used exactly once and never defined — it is presumably the Syncthing-shared checkout, but the sentence says the *proposal* is published *into the tree*, which reads as writing files into the synced directory. Unanswered: who reviews ("a reviewed proposal" is passive; §9's TUI view list at 630-631 has no publish/review view, only "security reviews" which line 96 ties to control files); does publish apply the patch or record intent; what applies it and where; what happens when two agents publish patches touching the same file (§8.3's Syncthing conflict machinery does not cover this — line 672 "File/worktree conflict | Preserve both" is the only hint and gives no mechanism); is publication a Raft-ordered strong event (no `worktree.published` kind appears anywhere).
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: This is the load-bearing sentence for the doc's central safety claim — that agents get filesystem isolation by default and integration is explicit and reviewed. An implementer will invent the entire protocol: one will `git apply` into the shared tree, another will emit an event carrying a diff and let a human run the merge, a third will `git format-patch` into `.codecomm/inbox/`. All three are consistent with the text and mutually incompatible on the wire and in the DB. Risk 10 (lines 977-978) admits this: "worktree publication needs reviewed ordering/conflict behavior" — the doc names the gap but does not close it.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Expand §7.2 with a ~15-line "Worktree publication" subsection: define "canonical synchronized tree"; give the event kind and payload fields; state whether publication is Raft-ordered; state who reviews it, in which TUI view, and with which CLI verb; state exactly what mutates the shared tree and under whose lease; and define the two-concurrent-publications outcome by reference to §8.3 or by a distinct rule.

cold-reader-runB.title: "eligible" and "up-to-date" are used as gating predicates with no definition, and "eligible" has two unrelated meanings
cold-reader-runB.quote: | Bootstrap | Verified Git bundle from any eligible up-to-date peer |
cold-reader-runB.problem: I grepped both terms. "Eligible" means peer-selection at 26 ("eligible up-to-date peer"), 571 ("an eligible up-to-date owner/editor source"), and 834 ("eligible replicas at the same committed index"), but means ignore-policy at 51 ("incrementally synchronize eligible workspace files") and 580 ("Syncthing overlays eligible dirty/untracked files"). Neither sense is defined. "Up-to-date" appears at 26, 372 ("Any up-to-date voter may serve a signed logical snapshot"), and 571, always as a precondition, never defined. The natural candidate definition — `applied_index == last committed index known locally` — is never written, and §5.3 line 363-364 establishes that applied index is tracked, so the machinery exists but the predicate does not.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: Line 372 is a correctness gate: a *not*-up-to-date voter serving a snapshot hands a joiner a stale projection that the joiner will then treat as a verified baseline and replay forward from, silently losing committed events between the snapshot's index and the real committed index. An implementer who reads "up-to-date" loosely (e.g. "has a leader" or "recently heard from the leader") will ship exactly that bug, and §12.3's convergence check at 834 uses the same undefined word, so the test would not catch it. On the bootstrap side (571), "eligible" silently decides whether a device that joined 30 seconds ago and has an empty worktree can be chosen as a bundle source.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Define both once, in §5.3 near line 371: "A replica is *up-to-date* when its applied index equals the highest committed index it has observed and it has heard from the current leader within one election timeout." Define bootstrap *eligibility* in §8.2 step 1 (role is owner or editor, up-to-date, has the workspace materialized, no unresolved conflicts). Rename the file-level sense at 51 and 580 to "included" or "non-ignored" so one word does not carry two meanings.

cold-reader-runB.title: §8.1 contradicts itself on whether the sidecar has a sync listener, and "connector" is undefined
cold-reader-runB.quote:
sync listener bind loopback only; the API uses a random owner-protected key and
pinned local certificate; GUI is not network-exposed.
cold-reader-runB.problem: Line 535 says the sidecar's sync listener binds loopback only — i.e. it exists and accepts connections on 127.0.0.1. Line 552-553 says "Disable Syncthing global discovery, relays, NAT/port mapping, direct TCP/QUIC listeners, introducers..." — i.e. no TCP/QUIC listener at all. In Syncthing config terms these are two different settings for `listenAddresses`: `tcp://127.0.0.1:<port>` versus `none`. The doc gives both. Separately, line 538-539 says "For each authorized owner/editor pair, Syncthing connects to a distinct local CodeComm connector" — "connector" appears exactly once in the file and is never defined; whether it is a per-peer loopback TCP listener owned by codecommd, a configured static device address of the form `tcp://127.0.0.1:<connector-port>`, or something else is left to the reader.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: The two readings produce different meshes. With `listenAddresses: none` on every sidecar, no sidecar can accept, so every one of the 28 pairs (line 546) must be dialed outbound by exactly one designated side — and the doc never says which side dials, which is a coordination rule that must be deterministic or pairs will either double-connect or never connect. With loopback listeners, the remote-forwarding side of line 540 ("which can forward only to its own session-bound loopback sidecar") works naturally but line 553 is violated as written. An implementer will pick one, and the other half of the mesh will silently fail to form on some pairs — exactly the kind of defect §12.3's fault list does not target.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Rewrite 552-553 to "disable non-loopback TCP/QUIC listeners" (or state `listenAddresses: none` and add the dialing rule), and add two sentences defining "connector": what object it is, what it listens on, how it appears in the sidecar's static device configuration, and which side of each pair initiates. A 6-line ASCII diagram of sidecar A -> connector A -> CONNECT tunnel -> daemon B -> sidecar B would remove the ambiguity outright.

cold-reader-runB.title: `inbox/` is an undefined untrusted input surface, absent from the security controls and security tests
cold-reader-runB.problem: I grepped "inbox": lines 393 and 426 are the only mentions. Line 426-427 adds "Inbox files are immutable, uniquely named, atomically renamed, and deduplicated by event ID" — which tells us the daemon *ingests* them and that they carry event IDs, so this is a second write path into replicated state alongside MCP and CLI. Nothing states who writes there, what schema is accepted, how the actor identity is established (§7.1 line 474 says "actor identity comes from the IPC binding" — a file in a directory has no IPC binding, so invariant "No agent identity spoofing" at line 94 has no enforcement mechanism here), what role check applies, what happens to malformed or oversized files, or whether the directory is ever drained. §10's control list (690-711) does not mention it. §12.4's security-test list (868-874) does not mention it. §12.2's unit subjects (802-812) do not mention it.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: As written this is a filesystem-based, unauthenticated proposal channel into the Raft log. Any process running as the user — including an agent that the doc explicitly treats as capable of ignoring workflow (risk 7, line 973) and as a prompt-injection target (line 684) — can drop a file naming any actor and any task transition. That directly defeats invariant 94 and the §7.1 promise that "No tool accepts... an actor ID". The word "optional" is doing a lot of work; nothing says it is off by default.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Either (a) delete `inbox/` from §6.1 and say submissions are IPC-only, or (b) add a ~8-line §6.x specifying it: default-off, owner-only directory mode, per-file size/rate caps, the exact accepted schema, how actor identity is bound (e.g. the file MUST carry an origin signature from an enrolled device key per §5.2 and the daemon MUST reject any actor not provable from that signature), drain/quarantine behavior, and add it to §10's control list and §12.4's security-test list.

cold-reader-runB.title: context.{json,md} / context.get content contract is never specified
cold-reader-runB.problem: I grepped `context\.(md|json|get)`: lines 392, 425, 467, 475, and the instruction at 486 ("MCP instructions require context refresh..."). We learn it is generated, atomic, read-only, non-authoritative, provenance-labeled untrusted data, and that `context.md` is a "read-only fallback" for `context.get`. We are never told what is *in* it. No field list, no size bound, no regeneration trigger, no statement of which projections it draws from.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: `context.get` is the primary mechanism by which an agent on device A learns what agents on B and C are doing — it is the actual delivery vehicle for the product's value proposition, and it is the one MCP call the doc tells agents to make first (line 486, "context refresh"). Two implementers will produce incompatible payloads (one dumps the task list; another dumps roster + current plan + peer activity + open conflicts + own leases), and the agent-facing instructions at 486-488 cannot be authored until the payload is fixed. It also blocks the golden-fixture requirement at line 816 ("MCP schemas/instructions") — you cannot golden-test an unspecified payload.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Add ~10 lines to §7.3 (or §7.1 after line 475) listing the `context.get` response fields with bounds: session/quorum summary, roster with roles, this agent's identity and leases, current plan revision digest, this agent's claimed tasks plus N ready tasks, recent peer activity capped at N entries with provenance, unresolved conflicts touching this agent's paths, and the applied index the snapshot was taken at. State the regeneration trigger and the guaranteed maximum size, and state that `context.md` is a rendering of exactly these fields.

cold-reader-runB.title: Task state machine is written as a linear arrow chain; real transitions, terminal states, and sync_blocked are unspecified
cold-reader-runB.quote: - Tasks: `backlog -> ready -> claimed -> in_progress -> blocked -> done`;
cold-reader-runB.problem: Read literally, `done` is reachable only from `blocked`, and there is no way out of `blocked` or back from `claimed` to `ready`. That cannot be intended, so the notation is not a specification. I grepped for the missing transitions: nothing anywhere describes unblocking, unclaiming, cancelling, or reassigning a task whose owning agent session ended — line 661 says agent disconnect releases "only its leases", which strongly implies a claimed task stays claimed by a dead `agent_session_id` forever, but the doc never says so or says otherwise. Separately, line 598 says CodeComm "marks affected tasks/agents `sync_blocked`" and line 600 says "scoped tasks cannot complete unresolved"; `sync_blocked` appears nowhere else — not in the task states at 431, not in the agent states at 498 (which have plain `blocked`). Whether `sync_blocked` is a sixth task state, an orthogonal boolean, or an alias for `blocked` is unknowable.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: This is a reducer specification, and reducers are required to be deterministic and identical on every replica (line 24, line 362 "stores the same structured rejection on every replica"). Two implementations that disagree on whether `blocked -> in_progress` is legal will diverge on projection digests, which is exactly the invariant §12.3 line 834-835 asserts ("equal projection digests"). The `sync_blocked` question is worse: if it is a state, then a Syncthing conflict overwrites the task's real state and the transition is unrecoverable; if it is a flag, the schema needs a column the table list at 405-406 does not mention.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Replace line 431 with an explicit transition table (from-state, to-state, required role, required actor binding) covering unblock, unclaim/release, cancel or abandon, and terminal states. State the fate of a claim whose `agent_session_id` ended. State whether `sync_blocked` is a separate boolean flag on the task row (and add it to the §6.1 table list) or a state value, and give its clearing condition.

cold-reader-runB.title: No alternatives-considered section: "why Raft at all for 2-8 personal devices" is nowhere on the record
cold-reader-runB.quote: | Strong state | Maintained embedded Raft; replaceable leader; 1/3/5 voters |
cold-reader-runB.problem: I grepped `alternativ|trade-?off|rejected|considered|CRDT|last-writer|coordinator|leaderless|gossip`: the only hits are line 19 ("no permanent coordinator", stated as a decision not a comparison) and line 729 (Rust vs Go, the one place a trade-off is actually weighed). §17 is an "ADR Backlog" — 21 titles, all phrased as the chosen answer ("ADR-001: Direct mTLS mesh and replaceable Raft leader"), and §13 phase 1 lists "threat model/ADRs" as future work. So every rationale is deferred to documents that do not exist, and the ADR titles pre-commit their own conclusions.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: Raft with joint consensus, a production stable store, snapshot handling, and quorum-gated credential authorization is the single largest cost and risk item in the doc — the author says so at risk 3 (lines 966-967: "Incorrect Raft transport/store/snapshot/membership/apply integration can violate safety despite using a mature library"). Yet the doc never argues against the two obvious cheaper designs for 2-8 personal devices: (a) CRDT/last-writer-wins with advisory leases and human conflict resolution, accepting occasional double-claims; (b) a single designated coordinator with manual failover. A reviewer cannot approve the highest-risk decision because its justification is absent, and the consequences of Raft cascade into hard constraints elsewhere — "two devices cannot tolerate one loss" (risk 2, line 965) is a real product limitation that only exists because of this choice.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Add §1.x or a new §16.x "Alternatives considered" of ~20 lines with three entries: CRDT/LWW + advisory leases; single designated coordinator with manual failover; hosted coordination service. For each, state the specific requirement it fails — cite the exact goal line, e.g. line 50 "preserve one winner for strong task/lease claims" — and the cost saved. Also add one sentence saying why exactly-one-winner is a hard requirement rather than a nice-to-have, since that is the sole justification for the entire consensus layer.

cold-reader-runB.title: The 9-step pairing, 6-step credential, and 8-step bootstrap flows are never mapped onto the REST endpoint table
cold-reader-runB.problem: §4.4 has 9 pairing steps and §5.1 offers exactly two pairing endpoints, with no mapping. Which endpoint carries step 5 ("The joiner proves the invite secret and submits its public identity")? Where does step 6's two-sided short-authentication-string comparison happen on the wire — is the SAS exchanged at all, or computed locally on both sides from the transcript and compared out of band by humans? (Line 223-225 says users compare it, which suggests out of band, but then `confirm` must carry *something*, and the doc never says what.) Step 8 ("receives membership proof, roster, and first credential authorization") plausibly maps to `GET /v1/peers` plus `POST /v1/credentials/renew`, but a joiner has no credential yet, and §4.5 step 3 says "Any voter forwards the request to the leader" — so which mTLS identity does the joiner present on that very first call? I grepped for a diagram or sequence: line 101-113 is the only diagram in the document and it is a static box drawing.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: Pairing and first-credential issuance are the security-critical bootstrap of every trust relationship in the system, and the chicken-and-egg question (what authenticates the joiner's first authorized request, given all post-pairing traffic requires mTLS with a quorum-committed key per lines 259-261) is left to the implementer. Getting it wrong here is the difference between a correct design and an unauthenticated enrollment endpoint. Two implementers will also produce incompatible wire protocols for the same nominal endpoint pair.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Add a sequence diagram (ASCII is fine, ~20 lines) covering invite creation -> `pairing/request` -> transcript/SAS -> `pairing/confirm` -> membership commit -> first credential authorization -> first authorized peer connection, annotating each arrow with the endpoint, the TLS identity presented in each direction, and what is verified. Do the same, more briefly, for the bootstrap flow in §8.2. State explicitly which endpoints accept a connection from a not-yet-committed device and what constrains them.

cold-reader-runB.title: Open questions contradict decided text and are not tied to a decider, date, or delivery phase
cold-reader-runB.quote:
2. **Plan authority:** May editors select current plan, or only propose for owner
   approval?
cold-reader-runB.problem: Open Q2 asks a question the doc has already answered twice: line 180 "| Make plan current | Yes | No by default | No |" and line 434 "editors propose by default, owners select". The phrase "by default" implies a configuration knob whose existence, storage location (the genesis "protocol policy" at line 168?), and change procedure are specified nowhere. Open Q1 pairs with line 593-595 "Ongoing commit/ref exchange, **if included**, MUST use an authenticated bare remote or incremental bundles" — so a whole feature is conditional, yet §13 phase 4 ("Git bootstrap") does not say whether it is in or out. Open Q5 (bundle Syncthing binaries vs download pinned artifacts) gates §13 phase 5 and the installer work in phase 6, and line 626 partially pre-answers it. None of the five questions names an owner, a decision deadline, or the phase it blocks.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: An implementation plan cannot be sequenced when a phase's scope depends on an unowned question. Q1 determines whether §8.3 needs a bare-remote subsystem at all; Q5 determines the installer, the SBOM, and the supply-chain review in §10 line 710. And the Q2/line-180 contradiction means an implementer will either build a configuration flag nobody specified or hardcode owner-only and be told later it was configurable.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: For each of the five questions add: the decider, the deadline, the delivery phase it blocks, and the default assumed if unresolved by that date. Reconcile Q2 with lines 180 and 434 — either delete Q2 and drop "by default" (making it a fixed rule), or state where the policy lives, who may change it, and whether changing it is a committed membership-class event.

cold-reader-runB.title: No glossary, and the doc's density makes forward references unresolvable on a single read
cold-reader-runB.problem: The document introduces roughly 30 project-specific terms and defines most of them implicitly, in place, and often after first use: strong/strict (line 20, never), trust epoch (143, never), connector (539, never), canonical synchronized tree (509, never), eligible / up-to-date (26, never), reducer (24, inferable only from §5.3), projection (361, inferable), watermark (282, inferable), capture_level (326, one example value, no enum), inbox (393, two clauses), collaboration (46/153, never). Line 8 supplies RFC-2119 conventions but no terminology section. The single diagram at 101-113 shows static component placement only.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: The stated bar is that no other context is needed. A cold reader currently has to build the glossary themselves by grepping backwards, which is what I had to do to review it, and several terms have no definition to find. New team members will each arrive at a slightly different vocabulary, and since the doc is normative (MUST/SHOULD), vocabulary drift becomes specification drift.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Add a §2.0 or appendix glossary of 20-25 one-line entries covering at minimum: strong operation, session, workspace, collaboration, trust epoch vs credential epoch, voter/nonvoter, eligible, up-to-date, reducer, projection, watermark, connector, sidecar, canonical synchronized tree, control file, capture_level (with its full enum), sync_blocked, inbox, genesis record. Cross-link each to the section that specifies it.

cold-reader-runB.title: §14 "Service Targets" are latency SLOs; there are no success metrics and no cost or timeline
cold-reader-runB.problem: I grepped `cost|timeline|week|month|quarter|milestone|success metric|adoption|kpi`: the sole hit is line 730 ("additional delivery cost" for the Rust option). §14 is entirely mechanism-level (p95 latencies, no-loss guarantees, exactly-one-winner). §13 lists six unsized, undated phases with no owners. There is no statement of how anyone will know this project succeeded.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: For the product half of the stated audience (line 6) there is nothing to act on and no way to sanity-check whether six phases of consensus, sync, and cross-platform hardening are worth it. It also means §14's own caveat — line 946, "Targets require benchmark validation before commitment" — has no counterpart for scope: nobody can say the project is done or overbuilt.
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Add a short §14.0 "Success criteria" separating outcome metrics (e.g. a two-device pairing completed by a first-time user in under N minutes without reading docs; X% of multi-device sessions with zero duplicated task work; zero silent file losses across the release soak) from the existing §14 performance targets. Add rough sizing and sequencing to §13 — even engineer-weeks per phase and which phases can run in parallel — and note the dependency on external artifacts (pinned Syncthing, MCP SDK, Raft library) surfaced in §11.

cold-reader-runB.title: References omit the specifications the design most depends on
cold-reader-runB.quote:
- Codex MCP: <https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp>
- Codex `AGENTS.md`: ...
- Git bundles: ...
- Raft paper: ...
cold-reader-runB.problem: The doc leans heavily on external behavior it does not restate: Syncthing conflict-copy naming and semantics (§8.3, lines 596-601), Syncthing ignore-pattern semantics (line 608-609 asserts "semantics differ" from .gitignore without citation), Syncthing staggered versioning (line 601), the Block Exchange Protocol (line 544), the MCP specification itself (§7.1), SPAKE2+ (line 232), and HTTP/2 extended CONNECT (line 271, 726). None is cited.
cold-reader-runB.why_it_matters: Minor on its own, but it is the one place where "no other context needed" is unachievable by design — the reader must consult these, and the doc does not say which versions or documents it was written against. Syncthing ignore semantics and conflict naming in particular are version-sensitive, and line 726 already commits to a "pinned Syncthing per OS/architecture".
cold-reader-runB.recommendation: Add five or six lines to §18: Syncthing docs for conflict handling, ignore patterns, versioning, and the Block Exchange Protocol (with the pinned version the design assumes); the MCP specification revision; the SPAKE2+ reference; RFC 8441 for extended CONNECT.

impl-readiness.title: Local IPC protocol is the highest-fanout interface in the system and is never specified
impl-readiness.quote: Only `codecommd` opens SQLite. CLI/TUI/MCP/hooks use local IPC. Core tables:
impl-readiness.problem: Local IPC is named in at least ten places but never defined. Genuinely absent (grepped for json-rpc/jsonrpc/framing/length-prefix/ndjson/unix domain): (a) framing and encoding, (b) the operation set and schemas, (c) versioning/negotiation between a CLI or MCP adapter and a daemon of a different build, (d) the handshake that establishes actor identity, (e) the error model, (f) socket path / pipe name derivation and per-workspace multiplexing, (g) the wire form of the "in-memory resume capability" (line 494). Line 261 ("Plain HTTP is limited to owner-restricted local IPC") hints at HTTP framing, but does not say whether the local surface is the same `/v1` REST surface from 5.1, a third surface, or something else. It cannot be the same: the MCP vocabulary at 466-470 (`task.claim`, `lease.acquire`) is a different shape from `POST /v1/events`, so a distinct local operation set must exist and is undocumented. Line 698 specifies only the *authorization* mechanism (peer UID / socket mode / named-pipe ACL), not the protocol.
impl-readiness.why_it_matters: Four consumers (CLI, TUI, MCP adapter, vendor hooks) and one producer (daemon) all bind to this interface, and two critical invariants are enforced at exactly this boundary: "No agent identity spoofing | Actor identity comes from the bound local MCP connection" (line 94) and "actor identity comes from the IPC binding" (line 474). Delivery phase 2 is "daemon/SQLite/reducers/local API/TUI; agent registry, MCP/CLI adapters" (line 918) - the first coding phase cannot be planned, split across people, or contract-tested. Two implementers will independently invent incompatible surfaces.
impl-readiness.recommendation: Add a subsection (e.g. 7.0 or 5.4) "Local IPC" stating: transport (HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over UDS / named pipe vs length-prefixed JSON-RPC), whether it reuses the `/v1` REST paths or defines its own `local/v1` operation set, the full operation list, the connect handshake that establishes `agent_session_id` binding, version negotiation and mismatch behavior (fail closed?), socket/pipe path derivation per workspace, error envelope, and the resume-capability representation. State explicitly whether the daemon rejects clients from a different build.

impl-readiness.title: No enumerated event `kind` registry, payload schemas, or per-kind reducer/authorization contract
impl-readiness.quote:
5. Every state machine applies it in index order and deterministically rechecks
   membership, signatures, actor binding, authorization, schema, sequence,
   transition, and expected version against prior committed state.
impl-readiness.problem: The envelope at 307-340 is fully specified, but `"payload": {}` is empty and only three `kind` values appear anywhere in the document: `task.updated` (322), `workspace.conflict.detected` (598), `control_file.change_proposed` (618). The action vocabulary at 346-347 is a different axis. Section 6.2 lists the state machines that must exist (tasks, plans, memory, leases, views) and section 3 lines 126-128 lists what Raft orders (task/lease transitions, current-plan selection, shared memory, membership/roles/voters/revocation, credential-key authorizations, durable audit events), but there is no mapping from `kind` to payload schema, to required application role, to expected-version/CAS semantics, or to reducer effect. Grep for dotted identifiers confirms no registry exists.
impl-readiness.why_it_matters: Step 5 requires every replica to deterministically recheck "authorization... transition, and expected version" per event - that check is per-`kind` and cannot be written without the registry. It is also the input to the hardest release gates: "deterministic projection rebuild" (805), "migration+replay digest" (819), "Immutable golden fixtures cover canonical events/batches/signatures" (815). Any divergence in kind semantics between two devices is a split-projection bug that the harness (835: "equal projection digests") will catch only after the fact. This is the single most load-bearing missing artifact in the doc.
impl-readiness.recommendation: Add a table enumerating every V1 `kind` with: payload schema (or a pointer to a schema file that is a V1 deliverable), minimum application role, whether it is strong (Raft-ordered) or ephemeral, entity type and whether `expected_entity_version` is required, and the reducer effect. Also state the canonical serialization used for signing (JCS-canonicalized JSON? CBOR deterministic encoding?) and the signature/hash algorithms - grep found no named primitive anywhere in the doc (no ed25519/ECDSA/HKDF/CBOR/JCS), only SHA-256 for Git bundles at line 572.

impl-readiness.title: 16 REST endpoints, one schema: no request/response bodies, status codes, error taxonomy, or pagination parameters
impl-readiness.quote:
All messages use explicit schema/capability versions, bounded pagination and
sizes, structured problem responses, and idempotency keys for mutations.
impl-readiness.problem: Lines 292-297 state policy, not specification. impl-readiness.title: Delivery phases have sequencing inversions, no exit criteria, no sizing, and no walking-skeleton path
impl-readiness.quote:

impl-readiness.problem: Three concrete problems. agents on the same or different devices and synchronizes their workspace.
cold-reader.problem: Section 1 is titled "Decision Summary" and opens with a one-sentence what-it-is followed immediately by a decision table. There is no statement of what breaks today, what workflow is currently impossible or painful, what a user does today instead, why local-first with no hosted service is required (privacy? air-gapped? cost? latency?), or what success looks like. cold-reader.title: Unresolved: is CodeComm one person's several devices, or several people collaborating?
cold-reader.quote: CodeComm is a local-first TUI/CLI and per-user daemon (line 12) ... 6. Both users compare and confirm a short authentication string (line 223) ... Same-user processes can bypass leases; identity does not provide filesystem isolation. (line 512) ... lost/compromised former members ... and workspace readability by authorized owner/editors. (lines 687-688)
cold-reader.problem: The doc points both ways and never decides on the record. Evidence for single-user/multi-device: "per-user daemon" (line 12, 43), "owner-restricted local IPC" (54), "owner-only locations" (401), "Same-user processes can bypass leases" (512), "A compromised local OS account ... outside the V1 boundary" (688). Evidence for multi-human: "Both users compare and confirm" (223), the entire owner/editor/observer privilege matrix (174-181), "cannot be self-granted" (183), "lost/compromised former members" (687), "workspace readability by authorized owner/editors" as a listed threat (688), and revocation as a first-class flow (668, 852). I grepped `personal|multi-user|single user|trust boundary` and found no sentence anywhere that resolves it.

If all devices belong to one person, the observer role, non-self-granting role changes, and "authorized owner/editors can read the workspace" as a *threat* are all pointless ceremony — and the reasonable critique "why Raft for my own three laptops?" becomes very hard to rebut. If devices belong to different people, then "per-user daemon" plus "identity does not provide filesystem isolation" (513) is a genuine security statement that needs to say clearly that a peer's agent output lands in your filesystem under your own OS account with no sandbox between you and their content, and §10's boundary exclusion of "compromised local OS account" (688) means something entirely different. The role matrix, the threat model, and the shared-root warning cannot be reviewed until this is fixed.
cold-reader.recommendation: Add an explicit "Users and trust boundary" subsection at the top of §2 (or as part of the new problem statement) stating in two or three sentences: whether V1 targets one operator's multiple devices, multiple humans, or both; what the trust relationship between members is (mutually trusting humans? one human's devices?); and one sentence on what an authorized editor can do to your machine that you are accepting. cold-reader.title: No alternatives-considered section: Raft, Syncthing, and mesh topology are asserted, never defended

Every other major decision is stated as a fact. §17 "ADR Backlog" (980-1002) lists 21 decisions by title, but they are a *backlog* — the ADRs do not exist yet, so there is currently no document anywhere that argues for Raft. Specifically absent: why consensus rather than a CRDT / last-writer-wins log with occasional manual reconciliation (the doc already accepts manual conflict resolution for files, per line 599-600, so the reader immediately wonders why task claims cannot be handled the same way); why not a single designated coordinator device with a documented manual failover (the doc already accepts that a lone survivor cannot make progress, line 61, which is close to what a coordinator gives you); why 30-minute credential rotation rather than longer-lived certificates with revocation; why Syncthing rather than periodic Git fetch between peers.

cold-reader.recommendation: Add a §"Glossary" immediately after the Decision Summary (a two-column table is enough) covering at minimum: strong state/mutation/claim, eligible (or better: split into `eligible peer`, `eligible file`, `eligible replica` and define each at first use), up-to-date (give the concrete predicate, e.g. "applied index within N of the committed index and not `sync_blocked`"), connector, canonical synchronized tree, credential epoch vs trust epoch (rename one — e.g. `trust_generation` — so the words cannot be confused), advertising key (state that it is the current credential epoch key), capture_level (enumerate the values), projection, reducer, watermark, sync_blocked, voter/nonvoter, genesis record.

cold-reader.title: `inbox/` is a second event-submission path with no stated authorization, apparently contradicting the actor-binding invariant

... Inbox files are immutable, uniquely named, atomically renamed, and deduplicated by event ID. (lines 426-427)
cold-reader.problem: `inbox/` appears exactly twice in 1010 lines (I grepped `inbox`), both times describing only its file mechanics. Never stated: who writes to it, what a "submission" contains, which component consumes it, and — critically — how actor identity is established for a file dropped there. "deduplicated by event ID" (427) says the contents are events, so this is an ingestion path into the replicated event log. But invariant line 94 says "No agent identity spoofing | Actor identity comes from the bound local MCP connection", and line 474 repeats "actor identity comes from the IPC binding". A file in a directory has no IPC binding and no MCP connection. Either inbox submissions cannot carry an `origin.agent_session_id` (in which case what actor do they get, and how does that square with line 345 "Agent-originated events require the bound agent session"?), or they can, in which case any process running as that OS user can forge any local agent's identity by writing a file — and the invariant at line 94 is false as written.

cold-reader.title: The mesh's most user-visible failure behavior (everything stops ~30 min after quorum loss) is stated only as a subordinate clause
cold-reader.quote:
Without a voter majority, strong mutations and new credential
authorizations MUST pause to prevent split brain, while local work and direct
sync among reachable peers continue only until current credentials expire.
cold-reader.problem: Reading this against line 238 ("a fresh TLS key authenticates each 30-minute epoch"), line 448 ("A minority may edit locally, queue events, and sync directly only while credentials remain valid"), and line 665 ("Quorum loss | Queue strong work; stop credential renewal"), the actual behavior is: lose quorum and within at most 30 minutes *all* peer-to-peer traffic in the minority stops — control API, SSE, and file sync — leaving each device fully isolated with a queue. That is the single most important operational fact about the system and it appears nowhere as a plain statement. As written the clause admits two readings an implementer will split on: (a) existing mTLS connections are torn down at expiry and no new ones can be formed, so the minority goes fully dark within 30 minutes; (b) only *new* connections are refused and established tunnels persist (line 252 "cap connection lifetime" hints at (a), but the cap value is never given). §9's failure table row for Quorum loss (665) mentions only strong work and renewal, reinforcing reading (b).
cold-reader.why_it_matters: Under reading (a) — which the credential design implies — a two-device session (explicitly permitted at line 60) that loses one device becomes a fully offline single machine within half an hour, with file sync dead. That is a product-defining limitation and it is not stated in §2.1 Goals, in §9's failure table, in §14 Service Targets, or in §16 Risks (Risk 2 at line 965 mentions only "Strong writes/renewal require quorum"). Under reading (b) a stale minority keeps two-way file sync indefinitely, which contradicts the "bounded stale access" security property at lines 254-255. An implementer must guess, and one of the two guesses is a security regression.
cold-reader.recommendation: Fix the ambiguity at line 35 with an explicit statement of the connection-lifetime cap, and add a dedicated paragraph either at the end of §1 or in §6.2 near line 449: "Quorum loss degrades in two stages: immediately, strong mutations and credential renewal pause; at most <cap> minutes later, all mTLS peer connections in the minority expire and cannot be re-established, so the minority devices operate fully offline with queued events until quorum returns or owner-approved recovery runs." Update the §9 Quorum-loss row and Risk 2 to say the same thing.

cold-reader.title: Line 6 claims a Product audience, but no section is usable by one; no success metrics, cost, or schedule

cold-reader.title: No policy for which devices become voters on join, and no explicit prohibition on even voter counts

| Strong state | Maintained embedded Raft; replaceable leader; 1/3/5 voters | (line 20)
